context: a letter from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
The Cucurbitaceous plant is Peponopsis adhærens, Naud. in Ann. Sc. Nat. Ser IV. 12. p. 89. of which he says “Cirrhis multifidis, in superficie vel lavissima adminiculorum extrema digitorum parte cohærentibus.” I send a copy of what he says further about it. Its native country is unknown, but as I am doing Cucurbitaceæ for Genera Plant. I do not despair of turning it up. Naudin describes it from cult specimen of ♀ plant. Welwitsch has a gigantic, climbing Scitamineæ from S.W. Africa.

I have read Sabines address in the Reader, it is very good on the whole but he has mutilated the Botany a good deal—especially the Linum & Lythrum bits, & clapped the beginning to the end of the Linum story, leaving out all the middle, in the funniest fashion. Lythrum he has literally dished.

He certainly has not praised you too much as to your Botany;—but I do suppose that your merits as Geologist, & Zoologist are Audaciously Exaggerated— there then

I send Huxleys account of his own proceedings.

I think the best thing of the kind I ever read in my life is Ruskin’s eloquent answer to big Jukes— it is delicious— Jukes may answer the letter, but not the man! who feels himself as far above J. as heaven is above earth—& is as far beyond the reach of knowing or learning or even seeing what is put before him by J. as we are of comprehending eternity.

Then too, “as one fool makes many” see M. A. Cs. small blue-light blazing up after reading Ruskin’s philosophy.

The cut at D’Isræli is capital too

Ever yrs affec | J D Hooker

Thanks for hints about queries to Hector, any number will be gratefully received.

Pray thank Mrs. Hooker much for her beautifully written copy from Naudin which is most useful to me. By the way Naudin has just sent me his Photograph.— what a nice looking man he is—with heaps of tournures about the Copley medal.—

What a curious case it is that one or two Bignoniaceæ Vitaceæ & Cucurbitaceæ should all develope adhesive discs at end of tendrils. I was thinking so this morning in my hot-house, & concluded that there must be incipient stages & so looked at the clasped tendrils of your Hanburya, & by Jove they form on under side a long narrow white cellular outgrowth which is strongly adhesive! The extreme cells are such curious objects with globular & retort-like heads.— Thanks, also, about the Scitamin: a new order to me.—

I return Huxley’s letter which I am glad to have seen. I think he was right pro bono publico; but I am sure I for one could not have dared to do so disagreeable thing.— Poor old Sabine is ill.—

I was charmed with Ruskin’s folly; & I see there is more to read today in the Reader; I missed the cut at D’Israeli. In one of his novels many years ago there are some splendid sneers at us transmutationists; a young lady saying “oh it is proved by geology” that we came from crows or something of the kind.— I see in foreign advertisements that a ‘Handbuch zur Physiologie” is coming out in 1865 by Hofmeister; I shd. think this would be so good that you ought to stir up some one to translate it. How goes on your Book on G. Distrib. of Plants? Do you make any progress? I fear not, you have so many irons in the fire & so many & such confounded correspondents like my blessed self.— It wd. not be worth my while to take in Bot. Zeitung & as I never go out I never see it; so will you ask Oliver, if he will be so very kind as to tell me if anything appear in it on Dimorphism that especially concerns me   I expect to hear of a paper Hildebrand on dimorphic Pulmonaria

signed C. Darwin.
